question_text: In a transformer, what does the self-attention mechanism primarily allow the model to do when processing a sequence?

options.1: Let each token gather information from other tokens, weighted by their relevance
options.2: Encode the whole sequence into a single fixed vector before the first layer runs
options.3: Read tokens strictly left to right, never comparing one token against another one
options.4: Swap each token for its closest dictionary synonym to normalize the input text first

explanation: Self-attention lets each token attend to other tokens in the sequence, weighting them by relevance so its representation captures context. It does not compress everything to one vector, read strictly left to right, or swap in synonyms.

question_text: A standard autoregressive language model generates text by doing what at each step?

options.1: Predicting a probability distribution over the next token given all preceding tokens
options.2: Predicting every token in the output sentence at once in a single parallel forward pass
options.3: Selecting a full sentence from a fixed list of memorized candidate responses each time
options.4: Filling in randomly masked tokens spread throughout the complete input sequence at once

explanation: An autoregressive model outputs a probability distribution over the next token conditioned on all previous tokens, then samples one and repeats. It does not decode the whole sentence in parallel, pick from a canned list, or unmask scattered tokens.

question_text: Why do transformer language models have a finite context window rather than accepting unlimited input length?

options.1: Attention compute scales with length and training used a fixed maximum length
options.2: The model keeps only one sentence in memory and throws away all earlier text later
options.3: Longer inputs are blocked because tokenization can handle only a few hundred characters
options.4: The output layer can emit just a fixed number of tokens, which caps the input length too

explanation: The window is finite because attention cost rises with sequence length and the model was trained with a fixed maximum length. It is not about storing one sentence, a character cap in tokenization, or the output layer size.

question_text: Byte pair encoding and similar subword tokenizers split rare words into smaller pieces mainly to achieve what?

options.1: Represent any word, including unseen ones, with a fixed, manageable vocabulary
options.2: Guarantee that each individual English word maps to exactly one whole-word token
options.3: Translate the input into another language before the model begins its processing
options.4: Remove all punctuation and spacing so the model sees only lowercase letter runs later

explanation: Subword tokenizers like BPE break rare words into pieces so a fixed vocabulary can represent any word, including unseen ones. They do not guarantee one token per word, translate the text, or strip punctuation.

question_text: In semantic search, why is cosine similarity between embedding vectors used to compare two texts?

options.1: Texts with similar meaning map to vectors pointing in similar directions
options.2: Cosine similarity counts how many identical words the two texts literally share
options.3: It measures the exact character-level edit distance between the two input strings
options.4: Shorter texts always score higher because the vector magnitude becomes much smaller

explanation: Cosine similarity compares vector direction, so texts with similar meaning map to vectors pointing similarly and score high. It is not literal word overlap, character edit distance, or driven by text length.

question_text: Retrieval-augmented generation reduces hallucination primarily because it does what?

options.1: Supplies relevant retrieved documents so answers can be grounded in real text
options.2: Retrains the model weights on the user question before producing any final answer
options.3: Lowers the sampling temperature to zero so the model can never make any mistake
options.4: Removes the language model entirely and just returns raw search hits to the user

explanation: RAG grounds answers by supplying relevant retrieved documents the model can rely on, which cuts invented facts. It does not retrain weights per query, zero the temperature, or drop the language model.

question_text: Why are long documents usually split into smaller chunks before being indexed for retrieval?

options.1: Smaller passages match queries more precisely and fit the context budget
options.2: The vector database rejects any document longer than a single short paragraph
options.3: Chunking permanently compresses the text so storage cost drops to almost nothing
options.4: Each chunk is translated separately, which improves the overall writing style later

explanation: Chunking yields smaller passages that match queries more precisely and fit the model context budget. It is not because databases reject long text, nor does it compress storage or improve writing style.

question_text: What is the primary role of a vector database in a retrieval system?

options.1: Store embeddings and quickly find those nearest to a query vector
options.2: Generate the final natural language answer shown directly to the end user
options.3: Convert user questions into SQL and run them against relational tables first
options.4: Compress the model weights so the language model loads faster at startup time

explanation: A vector database stores embeddings and efficiently finds those nearest to a query vector for retrieval. It does not generate the answer, run SQL queries, or compress model weights.

question_text: Chain-of-thought prompting tends to improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks because it does what?

options.1: Prompts the model to lay out intermediate steps before giving the answer
options.2: Forces the model to answer only in a single word so there is no confusion
options.3: Retrieves external documents that already contain the fully worked out solution
options.4: Increases the sampling temperature so the model explores far more creative guesses

explanation: Chain-of-thought asks the model to lay out intermediate reasoning steps before the answer, which helps on multi-step tasks. It does not force one-word answers, retrieve solutions, or raise temperature.

question_text: What distinguishes few-shot prompting from zero-shot prompting?

options.1: Few-shot includes worked examples in the prompt while zero-shot gives none
options.2: Few-shot permanently updates the model weights, while zero-shot leaves them fixed
options.3: Few-shot always uses a higher sampling temperature than zero-shot prompting does
options.4: Few-shot works only for images, while zero-shot applies just to plain text tasks

explanation: Few-shot prompting places worked examples in the prompt while zero-shot provides none; neither changes the weights. It is not about temperature settings, image-only use, or permanent updates.

question_text: In a chat-formatted prompt, what is the typical purpose of the system role message?

options.1: Set the overall behavior and constraints for the assistant
options.2: Contain the exact question the end user is asking on this current turn
options.3: Hold the model's previous replies so they can be echoed back to the user later
options.4: Store the retrieved documents that were fetched from an external knowledge base

explanation: The system message sets overall behavior and constraints guiding the assistant; the user message carries the current question and the assistant message holds prior replies. Retrieved documents are handled separately.

question_text: Why might a developer instruct a model to return its output as strict JSON?

options.1: So downstream code can parse the fields reliably without fragile scraping
options.2: Because JSON output makes the language model reason more accurately on hard problems
options.3: Because JSON output can never contain any factual mistakes or invented information
options.4: Because JSON responses are always shorter than the equivalent plain English answers

explanation: Strict JSON lets downstream code parse fields reliably instead of scraping free text. JSON formatting does not improve reasoning, prevent factual errors, or guarantee shorter output.

question_text: How do temperature and top-p sampling differ in how they control randomness during generation?

options.1: Temperature rescales the logits; top-p keeps only the top probability mass
options.2: Temperature edits the prompt wording, while top-p changes the model architecture
options.3: Temperature sets the output length, while top-p selects the language of the response
options.4: Both are identical settings, so changing either one has exactly the same effect anyway

explanation: Temperature rescales the logits to sharpen or flatten the whole distribution, while top-p keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probability mass reaches p. They are not identical, and neither edits the prompt or architecture.

question_text: When a RAG system attaches citations to its answer, what does this primarily let a user do?

options.1: Check the answer against the specific source passages that were retrieved
options.2: Confirm that the language model was retrained on the very latest available data
options.3: Guarantee the answer is correct because any cited answer is automatically true
options.4: See how long the model spent generating each sentence of the final response here

explanation: Citations point to the specific retrieved passages so a user can verify each claim against its source. They do not prove correctness, indicate retraining, or report generation timing.

question_text: Prompt injection is best described as an attack in which what happens?

options.1: Malicious text in the input tricks the model into ignoring its instructions
options.2: The database server is overloaded with traffic until it stops responding at all
options.3: Model weights are stolen and copied onto an attacker controlled server remotely
options.4: Random noise is added to embeddings so retrieval returns unrelated documents instead

explanation: Prompt injection hides malicious instructions in the input that trick the model into ignoring its intended instructions. It is not a traffic flood, weight theft, or embedding noise.

question_text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is primarily used to do what to a language model?

options.1: Align its responses with human preferences about helpfulness and safety
options.2: Expand its context window so it can read much longer documents at once
options.3: Teach it an entirely new natural language it was never exposed to before
options.4: Compress its parameters so it runs on much smaller devices than usual now

explanation: RLHF tunes a model so its responses align with human preferences about helpfulness and safety. It does not extend the context window, teach a new language, or compress parameters.

question_text: What is the core idea behind parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA?

options.1: Train a small set of added weights while keeping the base model frozen
options.2: Retrain every parameter of the base model from scratch on the new dataset
options.3: Delete unused layers so the network becomes smaller and faster to serve later
options.4: Replace the tokenizer with a custom one tailored to the target domain data set

explanation: LoRA and similar PEFT methods train a small set of added weights while freezing the base model, which saves compute. They do not retrain everything, delete layers, or replace the tokenizer.

question_text: For giving a model access to a frequently changing knowledge base, why is RAG often preferred over fine-tuning?

options.1: New documents can be indexed instantly without retraining the model weights
options.2: Fine-tuning is the only method that can ever change how the model behaves at all
options.3: RAG permanently bakes the facts into the weights so no storage is needed later on
options.4: Fine-tuning updates the stored knowledge automatically every time a document changes

explanation: RAG suits fast-changing knowledge because new documents are indexed instantly with no weight retraining. Fine-tuning would require a fresh training run for each change and does not update itself automatically.

question_text: In an LLM, where does knowledge supplied at inference time through the prompt reside, versus knowledge learned during training?

options.1: Prompt knowledge sits in the context window; trained knowledge is in the weights
options.2: Both kinds of knowledge are stored permanently inside the model weight matrices only
options.3: Both kinds live only in the prompt and vanish as soon as the current request completes
options.4: Prompt knowledge is saved to disk, while trained knowledge stays inside the prompt text

explanation: Prompt-supplied facts live in the context window for that request, while learned facts are encoded in the model weights. They are not both in the weights, both in the prompt, or swapped between the two.

question_text: In a retrieval pipeline, what is the purpose of a re-ranking step after the initial search?

options.1: Reorder candidates so the most relevant passages rise to the top
options.2: Translate every retrieved passage into the language used by the question
options.3: Delete the vector database once the first set of results has been fetched
options.4: Generate brand new documents to add into the knowledge base automatically now

explanation: Re-ranking reorders the initial candidates so the most relevant passages rise to the top before generation. It does not translate passages, delete the database, or create new documents.
